results.claim: Exact stationary rarity. For 0<p<1, put α=1-p. If π is the stationary law, then the complete-state probability is Π_{n,p}:=π([n])=∏_{r=1}^n [rα^r/(n-(n-r)α^r)]. Equivalently, R_{n,p}:=Π_{n,p}^{-1}=∏_{r=1}^n [1+(n/r)(α^{-r}-1)].
results.proof_sketch: The finite chain is irreducible, so its stationary law is unique and permutation invariant. For a fixed r-set A, write M_r=Pr_π(A⊆S), with M_0=1. After the draw, A is available either if it was already present or if exactly one member i was absent and the draw supplied i; then all r members must survive. Hence stationarity gives M_r=α^r[M_r+(r/n)(M_{r-1}-M_r)]. Solving gives M_r/M_{r-1}=rα^r/[n-(n-r)α^r]. Multiplication yields M_n=π([n]) and the first product. Taking reciprocals factor by factor gives [n-(n-r)α^r]/(rα^r)=1+(n/r)(α^{-r}-1).

results.claim: Finite-n hitting-time sandwich. Let H_n=∑_{j=1}^n 1/j and A_{n,p}:=(R_{n,p}-1)/(1-α^n). Then for every n and 0<p<1, A_{n,p}≤E[T_{n,p}]≤H_n A_{n,p}.
results.proof_sketch: Let h_k be the mean time to hit n from size k and e_k=h_k-h_{k+1}. Upward skip-freeness makes e_k the mean passage time k→k+1. A nested-set coupling of chains started at adjacent sizes preserves inclusion and leaves the upper set with at most one extra element, giving e_k≤e_{k+1}. Put u_k=(n-k)α^{k+1}/n and F_k(r)=Pr_k(K_1≤r). First-step analysis gives u_ke_k=1+∑_{r<k}e_rF_k(r). In the adjacent coupling, for every j≤k-2, ∑_{r=j}^{k-1}1{Y_1≤r}≥∑_{r=j}^{k-2}1{X_1≤r}. Taking expectations and applying Abel summation with the nonnegative increments of e_r shows that the recurrence numerator is nondecreasing. Since (n-k)e_k=nα^{-(k+1)} times that numerator, (n-k)e_k is nondecreasing. Thus h_0=∑e_k≤H_ne_{n-1}. Kac’s return identity at n gives R=1+∑_{k<n}Pr_n(K_1=k)h_k, with K_1∼Bin(n,α). Therefore A is a convex combination of h_0,…,h_{n-1}, conditional on leaving n. Hence e_{n-1}=h_{n-1}≤A≤h_0≤H_ne_{n-1}≤H_nA.

results.claim: Asymptotic closure throughout the non-classical range. For every fixed η>0, uniformly over η(log n)/n²≤p_n<1, E[T_{n,p_n}]=(1+o(1))A_{n,p_n}=(1+o(1))(R_{n,p_n}-1)/(1-(1-p_n)^n).
results.proof_sketch: The passage recurrence implies e_k/e_{k-1}≥F_k(k-1)/u_k≥k(1-α^k)/[(n-k)α^{k+1}], using the event that an already-held coupon is drawn and at least one held coupon is lost. Let m=⌊n/2⌋ and β=m(1-α^m). Uniformly in the stated range, β≥c_η log n: if mp≤1, then 1-α^m≥1-e^{-mp}≥mp/2; if mp>1, it is at least 1-e^{-1}. For a_j=e_{n-j}/e_{n-1} and J=⌊β/2⌋, the ratio bound gives a_{j+1}≤(j/β)a_j for j<J. Thus ∑_{j=2}^J a_j=O(β^{-1}) and a_J≤β^{-1}2^{-J+2}. Monotonicity of (n-k)e_k gives a_j≤Ja_J/j for j≥J, so the remaining sum is at most Ja_J(1+log(n/J))=o(1), uniformly. Consequently h_0/e_{n-1}=1+o(1). Since e_{n-1}≤A≤h_0, the claim follows.

results.claim: The resulting regimes differ from the product-of-marginals prediction. (i) If p=γ(log n)/n² with fixed γ>0, then E[T_{n,p}]∼n^{γ+1}/(γ log n). (ii) If (log n)/n²≪p≪1/n, then log E[T_{n,p}]∼n²p. (iii) If p=c/n with fixed c>0, then n^{-1}log E[T_{n,p}]→I(c):=∫_0^1 log(1+(e^{cx}-1)/x)dx>log(1+c). (iv) If np→∞, then log E[T_{n,p}]∼(n²/2)log(1/(1-p)).
results.proof_sketch: Write L=log R. Uniformly for p=o(1/n), α^{-r}-1=rp+O(r²p²), and summing log(1+(n/r)(α^{-r}-1)) gives L=n²p+O(n³p²). At p=γ(log n)/n², R∼n^γ and 1-α^n∼γ(log n)/n, proving (i). In (ii), L∼n²p→∞ and |log(np)|=o(n²p), so the denominator does not change the logarithmic equivalent. For p=c/n, the summands form a uniformly convergent Riemann array for f_c(x)=log(1+(e^{cx}-1)/x), continuously extended at zero, proving L/n→I(c). Since e^{cx}-1>cx for x>0, I(c)>log(1+c). Finally, with ℓ=-log α, exact factorization gives L=[n(n+1)/2]ℓ+nlog n-log(n!)+∑_r log(1-(1-r/n)e^{-rℓ}). The correction has absolute value at most ∑_{r≥1}-log(1-e^{-rℓ})≤(π²/6)/ℓ. If np→∞, then nℓ→∞, so this and the O(n) factorial term are o(n²ℓ), while 1-α^n→1. The preceding uniform theorem yields (iv).

final_writeup:
Put α=1-p and first suppose 0<p<1. The size chain K_t=|S_t| has one-step law

P_k(K_1=r)=(k/n)P(Bin(k,α)=r)+((n-k)/n)P(Bin(k+1,α)=r).

The stationary rare-event probability can be found without solving the chain. Finite irreducibility gives a unique, permutation-invariant stationary law. For a fixed r-subset A, let M_r=P_π(A⊆S). In one transition, A can be present only when it was already present, or when exactly one member was absent and the new draw supplied that member; all r members must then survive. Thus

M_r=α^r[M_r+(r/n)(M_{r-1}-M_r)],  M_0=1.

It follows that

Π_{n,p}:=π([n])=∏_{r=1}^n rα^r/[n-(n-r)α^r],
R_{n,p}:=Π_{n,p}^{-1}=∏_{r=1}^n[1+(n/r)(α^{-r}-1)].

We next compare this stationary rarity with the hitting time from 0. Let h_k be the expected time to hit n from level k, put h_n=0, and set e_k=h_k-h_{k+1}. Because upward jumps have size at most one, e_k is exactly the mean passage time from k to k+1. Couple chains from nested sets of sizes k and k+1 using the same drawn coupon and loss bits. Nesting is preserved and the upper set has at most one extra element. Hence the lower chain reaches k+1 no later than the upper chain reaches k+2, so e_k≤e_{k+1}.

Let u_k=(n-k)α^{k+1}/n=P_k(K_1=k+1) and F_k(r)=P_k(K_1≤r). Substitution of h_r=h_{k+1}+∑_{i=r}^k e_i into the first-step equation gives

u_ke_k=1+∑_{r=0}^{k-1}e_rF_k(r).  (1)

The same adjacent coupling, with one-step sizes X from k-1 and Y from k, has X≤Y≤X+1. Pointwise, for 0≤j≤k-2,

∑_{r=j}^{k-1}1{Y≤r}≥∑_{r=j}^{k-2}1{X≤r}.

After expectation, Abel’s decomposition

∑_{r=0}^q e_rF(r)=e_0∑_{r=0}^qF(r)+∑_{j=1}^q(e_j-e_{j-1})∑_{r=j}^qF(r)

shows that the numerator in (1) is nondecreasing in k. Therefore (n-k)e_k=nα^{-(k+1)} times this numerator is nondecreasing. In particular, e_k≤e_{n-1}/(n-k), and

h_0=∑_{k=0}^{n-1}e_k≤H_ne_{n-1}.  (2)

Kac’s identity supplies the other comparison. Starting at n, K_1∼Bin(n,α), and the mean first return time is R_{n,p}; hence

R_{n,p}=1+∑_{k<n}P_n(K_1=k)h_k.

After conditioning on K_1<n,

A_{n,p}:=(R_{n,p}-1)/(1-α^n)

is a convex combination of h_0,…,h_{n-1}. Since h_{n-1}=e_{n-1}≤h_k≤h_0, (2) proves

A_{n,p}≤E[T_{n,p}]=h_0≤H_nA_{n,p}.  (3)

The logarithmic gap in (3) disappears uniformly throughout the non-classical range. From (1), for k≥1,

e_k/e_{k-1}≥k(1-α^k)/[(n-k)α^{k+1}],  (4)

because F_k(k-1) includes the event that an already-held coupon is drawn and at least one held coupon is lost. Let m=⌊n/2⌋ and β=m(1-α^m). If p≥η(log n)/n², then β≥c_η log n: for mp≤1 use 1-α^m≥1-e^{-mp}≥mp/2, and for mp>1 use 1-α^m≥1-e^{-1}. Set a_j=e_{n-j}/e_{n-1} and J=⌊β/2⌋. Equation (4) gives a_{j+1}≤(j/β)a_j up to J, whence ∑_{j=2}^J a_j=O(1/β) and a_J≤β^{-1}2^{-J+2}. The monotonicity above gives a_j≤Ja_J/j for j≥J. Consequently

∑_{j=J}^n a_j≤Ja_J(1+log(n/J))=o(1)

uniformly, because β≥c_η log n. Thus h_0/e_{n-1}=∑_{j=1}^n a_j=1+o(1). Squeezing A between these quantities yields

E[T_{n,p}]=(1+o(1))(R_{n,p}-1)/(1-(1-p)^n)

uniformly for every fixed η>0 and η(log n)/n²≤p<1. This covers every non-classical regime in the source.

For completeness, let L=log R. If p=o(1/n), uniform expansion gives L=n²p+O(n³p²). It yields E[T]∼n^{γ+1}/(γlog n) at p=γ(log n)/n², and log E[T]∼n²p when (log n)/n²≪p≪1/n. If p=c/n, a Riemann sum gives

L/n→I(c)=∫_0^1log(1+(e^{cx}-1)/x)dx>log(1+c).

Finally, for ℓ=-log α,

L=[n(n+1)/2]ℓ+nlog n-log(n!)+∑_{r=1}^nlog(1-(1-r/n)e^{-rℓ}).

The last sum has absolute value at most π²/(6ℓ), while the factorial term is O(n). Thus np→∞ implies log E[T]∼(n²/2)log(1/(1-p)). These formulas disprove, rather than confirm, the product-of-marginals/mean-field prediction: at p=c/n its exponential rate is log(1+c), strictly below I(c). This replacement still fully resolves the target, whose preferred scale was conjectural. The excluded endpoints are elementary: p=0 gives nH_n, while p=1 gives T=∞.
